newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - "Club Med" countries say no EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - "Club Med" countries say no EMU delay.

text.p: Italy angrily rejected a report on Wednesday of plans to delay its membership of a single European currency and joined Spain and Portugal in insisting that hard economics should determine who gets in and who stays out.

"The Italian government...deplores the constant repetition of false stories and unjustified statements, including from authoritative media, which have no foundation whatsoever," a statement from Prime Minister Romano Prodi's office said.

It reaffirmed what Prodi called Italy's "solemn commitment" to meet the economic convergence criteria laid down in Europe's Maastricht Treaty for membership of Monetary and Economic Union (EMU) from the planned January 1, 1999 start date.
Prodi issued his statement after a Financial Times report that senior European central bankers and monetary officials were working on a plan to allow Italy in from 2000 or 2001.
The report called the purported plan a "face saving compromise" to assuage German fears that initial Italian entry would weaken the planned single currency, the euro.
It said the plan could be extended to other so-called "second wave" countries such as Spain and Portugal.
Both countries were quick to try to scotch renewed talk that their own efforts to prepare their economies for EMU could be held hostage to political considerations about Italian fitness.

"We are certain Spain is going to be where it should be, in the first wave of countries which constitute the European Monetary Union in the agreed timetable," Spanish Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro said.

The Portuguese Finance Ministry said each country's membership of EMU "can only be based on its own merits and on the objective evaluation of its ability to meet the convergence criteria defined in the treaty".

Prodi has pegged his political survival to first wave membership of EMU, inflicting bitter budgetary rigour on Italians and the prospect of more austerity in the run-up to a decision in early 1998 on which countries can join.
Insistent speculation of an Italian EMU delay has grown louder in the run-up to talks in Bonn on Friday between Prodi and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Kohl's Finance Minister Theo Waigel, France and the European Commission all denied on Wednesday that there was any plan to keep the lira out of the initial currency union.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini also backed Prodi, saying: "I absolutely exclude that there is a plan that aims to put Italy and other Mediterranean countries on the sidelines. I exclude it completely."

The statements, however, appeared unlikely to silence doubts about Italy's ability to meet one of the key qualifying criteria for EMU membership in 1999 -- a requirement to bring down the ratio of the public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent by the end of 1997.
Several senior German bankers have openly expressed fears that the sort of budgetary rigour Italy is adopting this year is not sustainable without deep structural reforms on spending.
But the risk, according to many economists, is that acknowledging too soon that Italy will not meet the conditions on time could hamper further belt-tightening by Rome.
"Any delay must involve a precise timetable and it (the delay) must not be too long. Even Spain needs extra time," said Renzo Avesani, chief economist at Italian savings bank Cariplo.
